# PREAMBLE

<br>

## Purpose of this session

<br>


During this training session, we will **integrate** a pair of samples into a single `SeuratObject` and into the same **multidimensional space**.

<br>

## The integration data set

We will still use data from the [Paiva et al.](https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(21)00281-3) publication.
    
While we focused on the **KO sample `TD3a`** until now, we will integrate it with its **wild-type** control counterpart **`TDCT`**.

`TDCT` was pre-processed in a very **similar manner** (QC, doublets, filtering) to what you performed for `TD3A`.

As the purpose is to **integrate** both samples into a single analytical entity, the objects we will use as input are `SeuratObjects` synced up to barcodes **filtering (bad quality, doublets)** (thus, there are no *dimension reduction* data in these objects)

<br>

# Connection to RstudioServer

To access RstudioServer on the remote HPC which we will work on, one must first connect to OpenOnDemand [here](https://ondemand.cluster.france-bioinformatique.fr){target="_blank"} using the documentation [here](https://doc.cluster.france-bioinformatique.fr/software/openondemand/getting_started/){target="_blank"}.

Once connected, the application to select is **Rstudio Server: Core**.

To create and/or join an Rstudio Server App, one can use the documentation [here](https://doc.cluster.france-bioinformatique.fr/software/openondemand/starting_rstudio_server/){target="_blank"}, with some modifications specific in the form to our training session :

-   **R version** : `4.5.2`
-   **Reservation** : `2621_eb3in1_2026`
-   **Account** : `2621_eb3in1_2026`
-   **Number of CPUs** : `2`
-   **Amount of memory** : `30G`    **Do not forget the "G" !**

Creation of the App will take a few seconds / minutes depending on the HPC workload.

Once create, the App will stay on as long as its dedicated time (`Number of hours`, **12** by default, and current maximum) are not over, and even if its browser tab is closed.

# Prepare the data structure

We will do as usual, just editing the session name
:

```{r}
#| label: create_struc
#| filename: create_struc

## PROJECT directory path
project_dir <- paste0("/shared/projects/", project_name)

## Test on PROJECT directory
if (dir.exists(project_dir)) {
  
  ## TD directory path
  TD_dir <- paste0(project_dir, "/SC_TD")
  
  ## SESSION directory path
  session_dir <- paste0(TD_dir, "/06_Integration")
  
  ##INPUT data directory path
  input_dir <- paste0(session_dir, "/DATA")
  
  ## OUTPUT data directory path
  output_dir <- paste0(session_dir, "/RESULTS")
  
  ## Creating the required directores
  dir.create(path = input_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = TRUE)
  dir.create(path = output_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = TRUE)
  
} else {
  warning("Provided project directory [", project_dir, "] does not exist !")
}
```

# Merge datasets

<br>

We simply merge the two objects into a single one :

```{r}
#| label: integr_merge
#| filename: integr_merge

TDCT_TD3A_merged <- base::merge(
  x = TDCT_so, # <1>
  y = TD3A_so, # <2>
  add.cell.ids = c("TDCT", "TD3A"), # <3>
  project = paste(c("TDCT", "TD3A"), collapse = "_")) # <4>
```

1.  First object to merge
2.  Second object to merge
3.  Keep track of sample of origin for cells (optional).<br>!! KEEP IT SYNCHED WITH YOUR (x, y) INPUTS !!
4.  Add a new project name (optional but recommended)

<br>

::: {.callout-note}
If you have more than 2 samples to merge, here is the way :

```{r}
#| label: multi_merge
#| filename: multi_merge
#| eval: FALSE

sobj_list <- list(sobj1, sobj2, sobj3, sobj4, sobj5) # <1>

sample_names <- c("S1", "S2", "S3", "S4", "S5") # <2>

MULTIMERGE <- base::merge(
  x = sobj_list[[1]], # <3>
  y = sobj_list[-1], # <4>
  add.cell.ids = sample_names, # <5>
  project = "MULTIMERGE") # <6>
```

1.  A **`list`** of `Seurat` objects (loaded into R)
2.  A **`vector`** of sample names (same length as `sobj_list`)
3.  The **first element** of the `sobj_list`
4.  **All but** the first element of the `sobj_list`
5.  The sample names
6.  The new project name
:::

<br>

::: {.callout-note}
We used the `base::merge()` function, thus the one natively packaged with R, but one can see that we used a parameter specific to `SeuratObject` : `add.cell.ids`, which can sound counterintuitive.

This is because the **base::merge()** function, while being a generic one **can be modified** in the shadows by additional packages, so that it adapts to **objects with new formats**.
:::

<br>

We can get a quick summary of the merged `SeuratObject` :

<br>

```{r}
#| label: merged_smry
#| filename: merged_smry

## A summary of the merged object
TDCT_TD3A_merged
```

<br>

::: {.callout-note icon="false" style="background: lightblue"}
## QUESTION 1A

What can you guess from the dimensions of `TDCT_TD3A_merged` on **the way it was merged** ?
:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true"}
## A HINT ?

To get to the answer, you'll have to **compare** its dimensions to those of the individual objects.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true" style="background: lightgreen"}
## ANSWER 1A

We check the dimensions of the three objects :

```{r}
#| label: dim_comp
#| filename: dim_comp

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Dataset = c('TD3A', 'TDCT', 'Merged'),
    Nrow= c(nrow(TD3A_so), nrow(TDCT_so), nrow(TDCT_TD3A_merged)),
    Ncol= c(ncol(TD3A_so), ncol(TDCT_so), ncol(TDCT_TD3A_merged))), 
  padding = 0,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ",")) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = "bordered",
    full_width = FALSE)
```

<br>

One can see that the **numbers of cells add up**, but **not those of features** !
:::

<br>
<br>

::: {.callout-note icon="false" style="background: lightblue"}
## QUESTION 1B

Thus, What can you actually guess **what happened for features** ?
:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true" style="background: lightgreen"}
## ANSWER 1B

We can compare the features in the individual and merged objects :

```{r}
#| label: featnames_comp
#| filename: featnames_comp

### Common features
feats_common <- intersect(
  SeuratObject::Features(TDCT_so), 
  SeuratObject::Features(TD3A_so))
message("Common features : ", length(feats_common))

### TD3A only
TD3A_specific <- setdiff(
  SeuratObject::Features(TD3A_so), 
  SeuratObject::Features(TDCT_so))
message("TD3A-specific : ", length(TD3A_specific))

### TDCT only
TDCT_specific <- setdiff(
  SeuratObject::Features(TDCT_so), 
  SeuratObject::Features(TD3A_so))
message("TDCT-specific : ", length(TDCT_specific))

### TOTAL
message("Sum = ", sum(length(feats_common), 
                      length(TD3A_specific), 
                      length(TDCT_specific)))
```

So, `Seurat` performed the **union** of the features from both individual objects
:::

<br>

::: {.callout-note}
This would remain true for **any number** of individual objects to merge !
:::

<br>

Now a bit of cleaning :

```{r}
#| label: merge_clean
#| filename: merge_clean

## Clean unneeded objects
rm(TD3A_so, TDCT_so, feats_common, TD3A_specific, TDCT_specific)
```

<br>
<br>

## Process the merged dataset

<br>

In order to visualize the data in a 2-D space, one needs to process it the way we learnt :

```{r}
#| label: merge_proc
#| filename: merge_proc
#| attr.output: '.details summary="Show output"'

## NORMALIZATION (LN)
TDCT_TD3A_merged <- Seurat::NormalizeData(
  object = TDCT_TD3A_merged, 
  verbose = FALSE)

## HVGs
TDCT_TD3A_merged <- Seurat::FindVariableFeatures(
  object = TDCT_TD3A_merged, 
  nfeatures = hvgs, 
  verbose = FALSE)

## SCALING + COVARIATES REGRESSION
TDCT_TD3A_merged <- Seurat::ScaleData(
  object = TDCT_TD3A_merged, 
  vars.to.regress = vars_to_reg, 
  verbose = FALSE)

## PCA
TDCT_TD3A_merged <- Seurat::RunPCA(
  object = TDCT_TD3A_merged, 
  npcs = pca_dims, 
  verbose = FALSE)
```

<br>

We keep a backup of this merged, processed object for later work :

```{r}
#| label: bak
#| filename: bak
#| 
TDCT_TD3A_bak <- TDCT_TD3A_merged
```

<br>

Elbow plot :

```{r}
#| label: merge_elbow
#| filename: merge_elbow
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-cap: "Elbow plot (merged)"

Seurat::ElbowPlot(object = TDCT_TD3A_merged, 
                  ndims = pca_dims, 
                  reduction = "pca")
```

We decide to keep the first **`20`** PCs.

```{r}
#| label: dims_kept
#| filename: dims_kept
#| 
dims_kept <- 20
```

<br>

## Visualization of the batch effect

<br>

### Covariates level

Here we will **assess** the **weight of covariates** on the first PCs, represented by :

-   Their absolute **Spearman correlation** score, for continuous covariates (like `percent_mt`, or marker genes expression), or :
-   The score of a [**Kruskal-Wallis**](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Test_de_Kruskal-Wallis) statistical test, for categorical covariates (like predicted cell cycle phases, by ex.).

```{r}
#| label: merge_acov
#| filename: merge_acov
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-cap: "Covariates weight on PCs (pre-post regression)"

## Assessing un-regressed data ("data" layer as proxy)
AC1 <- assess_covar(
  mat = as.matrix(SeuratObject::LayerData(
    object = SeuratObject::JoinLayers(TDCT_TD3A_merged, assay = "RNA"),
    assay = "RNA",
    layer = "data")),
  covar.df = TDCT_TD3A_merged[[]], 
  markers = cell_markers, 
  ndim = 10L, 
  center = TRUE, 
  scale = TRUE, 
  plot = FALSE, 
  title = "Normalized", 
  return.weights = FALSE, 
  return.plot = TRUE)

## Assessing regressed data (scaled)
AC2 <- assess_covar(
  mat = SeuratObject::LayerData(
    object = TDCT_TD3A_merged, 
    assay = "RNA", 
    layer = "scale.data"), 
  covar.df = TDCT_TD3A_merged[[]], 
  markers = cell_markers, 
  ndim = 10L, 
  center = FALSE, 
  scale = FALSE, 
  plot = FALSE, 
  title = "Scaled", 
  return.weights = FALSE, 
  return.plot = TRUE)

## Stack plots
cowplot::plot_grid(
  grid::grid.grabExpr(ComplexHeatmap::draw(AC1)),
  grid::grid.grabExpr(ComplexHeatmap::draw(AC2)), 
  ncol = 1, 
  align = "v")
```

::: {.callout-note icon="false" style="background: lightblue"}
## QUESTION 2

What can you observe and guess from these heatmaps ?

Namely, on the consequences of the covariates regression on the weight of themselves, others, markers ?
:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true" style="background: lightgreen"}
## ANSWER 2

Solely based on these heatmaps, one can observe that the regression of covariates :

-   **Reduced their weight** on the PCA space for the **very first components** (but slightly increased in later ones)

-   Did **not annihilate** the weight of **marker genes** expression, even seems to have **globally increased** it, and more especially for some specific genes (Pbk, Esco2, Trbv29, C1qa, Lyz2)
:::

<br>

### UMAP reduction level

<br>

Same, in the UMAP space :

```{r}
#| label: merge_umap

## Computing the UMAP space

  seed = my_seed, 
  dims = 1:dims_kept, 
  verbose = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: merge_umap_dp

print(Merged_dp)
```

<br>

::: {.callout-note icon="false" style="background: lightblue"}

Give your interpretation of this plot : Do you consider the samples as perfectly integrated ? And why ?

# Sample-aware regression

<br>

If covariate regression allows to reduce sources of bias, why wouldn't we consider the **sample of origin as** one of these **adversarial covariates**  ?

Let's try !

<br>

## Reprocessing

<br>

::: {.callout-note icon="false" style="background: pink"}
## DEMO

Re-processing, this time adding the **sample name** as a **new covariate** to regress :

```{r}
#| label: sample_regr_proc
#| filename: sample_regr_proc
#| attr.output: '.details summary="Show output"'

## NORMALIZATION (LN)
TDCT_TD3A_sreg <- Seurat::NormalizeData(
  object = TDCT_TD3A_bak, 
  verbose = FALSE)

## HVGs
TDCT_TD3A_sreg <- Seurat::FindVariableFeatures(
  object = TDCT_TD3A_sreg, 
  nfeatures = hvgs, 
  verbose = FALSE)

## SCALING + COVARIATES REGRESSION
TDCT_TD3A_sreg <- Seurat::ScaleData(
  object = TDCT_TD3A_sreg, 
  vars.to.regress = unique(c('orig.ident', vars_to_reg)),       # <1>
  verbose = FALSE)

## PCA
TDCT_TD3A_sreg <- Seurat::RunPCA(
  object = TDCT_TD3A_sreg, 
  npcs = pca_dims, 
  verbose = FALSE)
```

1.  Here we add the sample name (`orig.ident`) as a new covariate to regress

<br>

Elbow plot :

```{r}
#| label: sample_regr_elbow
#| filename: sample_regr_elbow
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-cap: "Elbow plot (sample-regressed)"

Seurat::ElbowPlot(object = TDCT_TD3A_sreg, 
                  ndims = pca_dims, 
                  reduction = "pca")
```
:::

<br>

## Effect of the regression

### Covariates level

<br>

We can observe the remaining weight of covariates after this special regression :

::: {.callout-note icon="false" style="background: pink"}
## DEMO

```{r}
#| label: sample_regr_acov
#| filename: sample_regr_acov
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-cap: "Covariates weight on PCs (w, w/o sample regression)"

## Assessing the covariates weight after regression
AC3 <- assess_covar(
  mat = SeuratObject::LayerData(
    object = TDCT_TD3A_sreg, 
    assay = "RNA", 
    layer = "scale.data"), 
  covar.df = TDCT_TD3A_sreg[[]], 
  markers = cell_markers, 
  ndim = 10L, 
  center = FALSE, 
  scale = FALSE, 
  plot = FALSE, 
  title = "Scaled, sample-regressed", 
  return.weights = FALSE, 
  return.plot = TRUE)

## Comparison to the simple merge
cowplot::plot_grid(
  grid::grid.grabExpr(ComplexHeatmap::draw(AC2)),
  grid::grid.grabExpr(ComplexHeatmap::draw(AC3)), 
  ncol = 1, 
  align = "v")
```
:::

<br>

### PCA reduction level

<br>

How do our sample pair cells mix up in the PCA space ?

::: {.callout-note icon="false" style="background: pink"}
## DEMO

```{r}
#| label: sample_regr_pca
#| filename: sample_regr_pca
#| fig-align: "center"
```

### Harmony (PCA embeddings)

Harmony can also be run on PCA embeddings directly.

This is useful when not working with a `SeuratObject`.

::: {.callout-important icon="false" style="background: pink"}
## DEMO

<br>

**Integration**

```{r}
#| label: integr_harmony_pca
#| filename: integr_harmony_pca
#| attr.output: '.details summary="Show output"'

## Fixing the seed
set.seed(my_seed)

## Running Harmony on the PCA reduction, limited to the selected first PCs
HS1 <- harmony:::RunHarmony.default(
  data_mat = SeuratObject::Embeddings(
    object = TDCT_TD3A_merged, 
    reduction = "pca")[,1:dims_kept], 
  meta_data = TDCT_TD3A_merged[[]],
  vars_use = "orig.ident",
  verbose = FALSE)

## Injecting the newly created harmony embedding into the SeuratObject
TDCT_TD3A_merged[["harmony_pca"]] <- Seurat::CreateDimReducObject(
  embeddings = HS1, 
  key = "harmonyS1_", 
  assay = Seurat::DefaultAssay(TDCT_TD3A_merged))

## Cleaning
rm(HS1)
```

## Unified plot

### Samples

```{r}
#| label: unified_samp
#| filename: unified_samp
#| fig-width: 15
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-cap: "Aggregation of UMAP for all methods (Samples)"

Merged_dp + SampReg_dp + 
  Harmony_samp_dp + S.CCA_samp_dp + 
  S.RPCA_samp_dp + S.Harmony_samp_dp + 
  patchwork::plot_layout(ncol = 3)
```

<br>

::: {.callout-note icon="false" style="background: lightblue"}
## QUESTION 6

Based on the observation and comparison of these UMAPs, which method would you choose, and why ?
:::

<br>

::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true" style="background: lightgreen"}
## ANSWER 6

What we can observe for each (kinda a summary), for this experiment

-   Simple merging provides insufficient quality of integration (numerous parts of the topology seem to be mirrored in both samples).

-   Regressing the sample of origin as a covariate provides a slightly better integration, but gives a strange topology inside putative clusters, where both samples do not mix well.

-   At first glance, Seurat CCA seems to perform way better than these two first naive approaches. However, their is still some awkwardness in the topology/mixture of samples, and clusters do not seem as well defined as other methods.

-   Seurat RPCA seems to provide an other level of mixing of the pair of samples.. maybe a bit *too much* of a mixture in this case : with the exception of the soutern cluster, almost all other structures seemed relatively balanced across both samples. We may be in a case of *over-fitting*.

-   Seurat's Harmony wrapper results show a topology with apparently well-defined clusters, some of which exhibit clear sample-specificity.

-   Harmony run as standalone also shows well-defined clusters, some of which are clearly sample-specific.

<br>

**However** :

-   These observations are limited to the outline of the topology in an (extremely) reduced space, and without taking into account neither of the sub-levels of this topology (*clusters*, answered below) nor any **biological knowledge** (expected cell populations and their sample specificity, answered in the next training session)

-   Without these other observations / pieces of knowledge, it is hard to distinguish between sample-specificity or lack of fitting, as well as between true community or over-fitting.

:::

<br>

### Clusters

```{r}
#| label: unified_clust
#| filename: unified_clust
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-cap: "Aggregation of UMAP for all methods (Clusters)"

S.CCA_dp + S.RPCA_dp + 
  S.Harmony_dp + Harmony_dp + 
  patchwork::plot_layout(ncol = 2)
```

<br>

::: {.callout-note icon="false" style="background: lightblue"}
## QUESTION 7

Adding these observations to the former ones, which method would you actualy choose, and why ?
:::

<br>

::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true" style="background: lightgreen"}
## ANSWER 7

-   Harmony standalone space seems to provide the most well-defined Leiden clusters of all (no split, quite clean outline, not too much outliers).

-   Harmony through Seurat is close, with a bit of noise above clusters 1, 5 and 3.

-   Seurat RPCA clusters seem roughly fine, with a bit of noise.

-   Seurat CCA clusters are the worst of the batch, with cluster 10 split into two parts, and with outliers quite everywhere.

<br>

**However** :

-   The same resolution was used for all spaces : the value was probably not optimal for all of them.

-   Remember that the UMAP space is an extreme approximation of a much more complex space : its 2-D topology may not perfectly reflect the intrinsic biology !

- In conclusion, we really need additional information, this time provided by biological knowledge. This will be treated in the next training session !
:::

<br>
<br>

::: {.callout-note}

**Why are there differences between Harmony called by Seurat and standalone ?**

This is a question of **different default parameters**.

:::: {.columns .with-divider}

::: {.column width="50%"}
Here is an excerpt of the help for the `Seurat::HarmonyIntegration` wrapper function to Harmony :

```
Seurat::HarmonyIntegration(
  object,
  orig,
  features = NULL,
  scale.layer = "scale.data",
  new.reduction = "harmony",
  layers = NULL,
  npcs = NULL,
  key = "harmony_",
  theta = NULL,                 ## SAME
  lambda = NULL,                ## SAME
  sigma = 0.1,                  ## SAME
  nclust = NULL,                ## SAME
  tau = 0,                      ## SAME
  block.size = 0.05,            ## SAME
  max.iter.harmony = 10L,       ## SAME
  max.iter.cluster = 20L,       ## ! DIFF !
  epsilon.cluster = 1e-05,      ## ! DIFF !
  epsilon.harmony = 0.01,       ## SAME
  verbose = TRUE,
  ...
)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
And here is the same for Harmony standalone :

```
harmony::RunHarmony(
  data_mat,
  meta_data,
  vars_use,
  theta = NULL,                   ## SAME
  sigma = 0.1,                    ## SAME
  lambda = NULL,                  ## SAME
  nclust = NULL,                  ## SAME
  max_iter = 10,                  ## SAME
  early_stop = TRUE,
  ncores = 1,
  plot_convergence = FALSE,
  return_object = FALSE,
  verbose = TRUE,
  .options = harmony_options(),
  ...
)
```

Some parameters are missing here : they are available as **global options**, accessed with `harmony::harmony_options()` :

```
> harmony::harmony_options()
$alpha
[1] 0.2             ## !!! UNK !!!
$tau
[1] 0               ## SAME
$block.size
[1] 0.05            ## SAME
$max.iter.cluster
[1] 4               ## ! DIFF !
$epsilon.cluster
[1] 0.001           ## ! DIFF !
$epsilon.harmony
[1] 0.01            ## SAME
$batch.prop.cutoff
[1] 1e-05           ## !!! UNK !!!
```
:::

:::

This is most probably to **maintain compatibility** of the wrapper with the 1st generation of the `Harmony` method (v1.x).

:::
